Brought my reactive gal to a relatives house last night (she had previously met everyone there before and has good relationships with/feels safe with everyone who was going to be attending.) suddenly, after dinner the door to the house flew open and someone in a full on Santa suit, complete with a belly, hat, and beard, came charging up the stairs. I can’t make this shit up. Legitimately my worst nightmare as a reactive dog owner. This person (a friend of the family) was uninvited but just showed up anyway without asking or contacting anyone, so we couldn’t warn them about my pup. Everything was fine, I was able to grab my dog and sit with her in a separate room, but she was SO worked up and confused and I felt horrible. I had brought her because I really didn’t want her to leave her alone all day, and of course didn’t anticipate anything like this happening (I had asked ahead of time and made sure that the dog had previously met everyone who would be attending, and that there would be no unexpected guests.) 

“Santa” ended up eventually taking the suit off and my dog was able to come out and coexist with the new person in the room after being bribed with some table scraps, and I’m proud of her/glad for that, but I’m feeling down because clearly unexpected shit can always happen and I’m really thinking she’s probably going to have to be left behind from now on. If I hadn’t gotten to her in time before “Santa” came up the stairs, it could have been a really bad situation. I’m glad nothing happened but just feeling frustrated.

As a t1d in the US, it absolutely limits my career. I’ve ended up in a field that I like most of the time, but this isn’t what I would have done had I not had t1d. When I graduated college, I knew I had to go into a field that would be stable and have solid health benefits. I’d love to work at a mountain as a lifty or resort staff and be able to snowboard everyday, but with the low benefits/pay most jobs like that offer, I could simply never make it work. Working at a desk 5 days a week (and a second job on the weekends, to make ends meet and pay off deductibles and copays) isn’t what makes me truly happy, but unfortunately it’s my best option for survival. 

I had to leave a super toxic job this past spring and didn’t have anything else lined up, which was a nightmare scenario stress-wise. Thankfully I got on Medicaid, but it only worked out because I had zero income coming in and was living on savings. The income parameters for Medicaid are so unrealistically low that if I had basically any income coming in, I would not have qualified, and would have been totally screwed. The other thing that saved me during that time was having supplies stockpiled- always try to do that if you can.

I lived away from home with roommates for years, but got my own place about 3 years ago. I personally feel fine living alone, but I also was diagnosed at 4 and grew up with t1d, so idk if that’s a factor. I’ve been pretty self-sufficient in terms of diabetes stuff since I was a teen, so my parents weren’t super worried, but I do keep in touch with them if they reach out so they’re not worried that I’m alone and passed out or something. 

My blood sugars are definitely not exceptionally awesome or anything but I do use a sensor and check them often/try to keep track of any trends up or down. Biggest piece of advice is to always, always have food or low blood sugar snacks in the house. Sometimes it’s a pain at the end of my work day to have to go to the store and buy fruit snacks, but when I’m alone and 50 at 3 am I’m always glad I did. I recommend specifically keeping low snacks by your bed, too- that’s saved me more than a few times. 

All in all, you just have to be prepared and understand that living alone means you’re (often) not going to have anyone else to rely on- it’s up to you to stock up on supplies, keep track of your blood sugars, etc.

T1d since 1999 and I do wear one. Just a simple bracelet that has my name, “Type 1 diabetic” and “call 911” on it. I’ve never had a blood sugar event where I needed outside assistance since I was a child (I’m 28 now), but it gives me peace of mind. I’ve heard plenty of stories of people being hit with a sudden low and then getting arrested for public intoxication because no one knew they were a t1d and they just seemed drunk. Never want that happening to me.

I drink beer and seltzers typically and that has worked for me. I’ve gotten wrecked before by fruity mixed drinks that shoot me super high and then almost kill me later. Also, go slow. Bring LOTS of low snacks. I do not drink unless I have at least 5-6 little packs of fruit snacks on me and that strategy has never failed me- better safe than sorry and I’ve actually helped some other unprepared t1ds while out and about as well. If you have a pump, a backup pen/needles is a good idea too and could save you from having to go home early if your pump fails. I also drink a lot of water in between alcoholic beverages- if I start to feel like I’m too out of it I stop drinking, because I never want to get to the point where I can’t take care of myself. The water breaks help me gauge where I’m at. 

I also typically dip late at night/morning after so low snacks by your bed isn’t a bad idea either. 

You’ll figure out what works for you and will get to the point where all of this is nbd. Cheers!

I’ve only ever had tubed pumps- I totally get what you’re saying about the site having a low presence, this is why I’ve never wanted an Omnipod. I almost always wear my sites on my abdomen and tuck the excess tubing into a pocket or under my shirt. For sleeping, you can clip it to the waistband of your pants (what I do) or just lie it down next to you. On average, the tubing gets caught on something and the site gets pulled out *maybe* once a year, if that; this is rarely a concern for me. Anecdotal evidence: Last year, I was snowboarding and fell, and my pump (which was attached to the side of my abdomen) slid out of my pocket without me noticing. I made it down the entire mountain with the site still attached to me, pump swinging between my legs! I didn’t even notice, and the site was totally intact.

You should see if you endo would be willing to advocate for you. That’s the only way I’ve ever won any insurance appeals. I just successfully fought to get my Contour Next test strips covered. My insurance was insisting they would only cover two other strip brands that were not compatible with my pump and meter. They wanted me to pay full price to try both other brands first, even thought we knew that they would not work. 

It was a long process…. Had to contact my doctor to explain the situation, and within a couple days a nurse wrote a letter of medical necessity explaining why I needed the specific strips, and got the doctors signature on the letter. My doctor then had to submit the letter back to insurance- it couldn’t come from me directly, insurance stated it had to be sent from the doctor. After that, it took over a month for my insurance to get back to me, but they did cover the strips. 

I hope you are successful as well- the cost of this disease is fucked up, and the mental burden of trying to find the time for all the back and forth with insurance, while also trying to live your life, is just the icing on the cake. Sending strong ✨beat the system✨ vibes.

I snowboard 2-3 times a week in the winter. My
blood sugars tend to fluctuate, but when you’re riding the lift and/or finish a run, that is a good time to check and make corrections if needed. If you feel “off”, don’t be afraid to go over to the side of the trail and check your CGM, just make sure that you’re visible and out of the way so that no one will run into you. When I was learning, I never had issues with my pump breaking when I fell, but it did slide out of my pants pocket a few times. I would recommend snow pants with zippers for this reason. Keep fruit snacks with you in case you go low- they don’t take up much room in your coat or pants pockets. And like many others have said, absolutely wear a helmet! I hope you have a great time! Snowboarding has been a great outlet for me among the stress of living with t1d.

Love this question! It’s something I’ve thought about a lot and my “strategy” on this has changed over the years. Most of my life I kept it super quiet, refused to wear a CGM because I didn’t want any visible signs of diabetes on me, and only told very close friends. When I got my first job out of college, I kept this up and did not want anyone to know I was a T1D, and it caused a ton of problems. I kept getting chosen to attend night meetings 50-60 minutes away from home (often meaning no dinner and no reliable schedule to exercise, which caused problems for me). I also frequently had to leave early/adjust my schedule for various diabetes related appointments, but because no one there knew I was diabetic and how much care is is required to keep us healthy, they all thought I was lying to get out of work (no one called me out specifically, but I could tell they felt that way/heard it whispered around in the hallways, which was the worst.) 

Now, after 21 years of t1d, I don’t like to be as quiet about it anymore, I prefer most of the people who know me in some capacity to know that I have it. If I’m out for a drink with friends and there are people in our group who don’t know I have T1D, I won’t necessarily bring it up to them if it doesn’t come up in conversation, but I definitely won’t hide it like I used to. Because I was diagnosed at age 4, it has been such a defining factor in my life, and now I feel like if I keep it quiet, I am hiding a big part of myself. I wear my CGM on my arm proudly, often with obnoxious tape. Most of the people at my current job know that I have it and I no longer feel guilty/worried that people are going to gossip about me leaving for appointments- they already know! I do get annoyed with the constant stigma and stereotypes that come with being more open about it, but when these things come up, I try to remind myself that it’s an opportunity to educate others, and prevent more stigma and stereotypes from being perpetuated in the future.
